title: 2  Kiribati BioMarkers Pipeline Operator’s Manual
text:
This manual composes and runs the entire pipeline for cleaning, curating, and distributing our Kiribati BioMarkers datasets. The intended audience for this document is:

Developers/data scientists who need to run the pipeline to produce outputs
Developers/data scientists who need to add features
Reviewers who need to ensure the accuracy and validity of the pipeline.

The /notebooks directory provides the Quarto Manual, which is a human-facing interface for “operating” the pipeline. Following the pages step-by-step allows readers to:

Recreate the computational environment necessary for running the pipeline
Understand the logical flow of data from source to output
Identify key decision points in analysis and data curation
Scrutinize the codebase without having to run it locally
Reproduce the pipeline on your own cluster or machine

title: 3  Render In Isolation
text:
3.1 Profiles
The first page of our project establishes Quarto as our human-readable engineering surface. This makes use of our Quarto Manual workflow.
Quarto has a notable limitation that we’re still investigating. The gist is that we can’t seem to have multiple renders running smoothly on the cluster, causing odd errors that are hard to debug.
Use scripts/render-isolated when another Quarto render may be using this checkout. It stages a private copy of the repository on the node-local temporary filesystem, so each render owns its own notebooks/.quarto/_freeze directory and Quarto cache. Only a successful rendered site is copied back to the shared checkout.
Run the generated wrapper from the repository root. Any arguments after the script name are forwarded to quarto render notebooks:
Quarto profiles keep the three kinds of work in this project explicit: authoring is the default for reading, editing, and previewing the Manual; it renders the site without loading the file-emission extension. emit loads that extension and materializes the scripts and configuration described by the Manual. Both profiles disable code execution completely: rendering and emission are host-side documentation operations, not scientific computation.
They are separate because these operations have different side effects and review expectations. An ordinary authoring render should be safe to repeat without unexpectedly changing generated files or processing data. Emitting files is an intentional, reviewable synchronization from the Manual to its derived artifacts.
The isolated wrapper promotes files recorded by Quarto-emit’s manifest after a successful render, so an emit render updates the Manual’s generated scripts and configuration in the checkout. It does not run targets or promote arbitrary data products. Run scientific work separately through the container runner after reviewing the emitted targets graph.

title: 3  Render In Isolation
text:
At the end of a project render, Quarto prunes its freeze directory. Two processes pruning the same notebooks/.quarto/_freeze tree can race: one sees entries that the other has already removed, which can surface as Directory not empty. The staged copy gives each render a separate tree, so the prune operation has no shared mutable directory to remove.


Materialize the script and check its syntax:
quarto render notebooks --profile emit --no-execute
bash -n scripts/render-isolated
Confirm that scripts/render-isolated begins with the generated-file provenance header. The manual page, rather than the generated script, is the source of truth.

title: 4  Project Contract
text:
This page defines the different components of the project and emits those necessary, focusing primarily on folder creation and assignment.
The project initially uses the Cookie Cutter Data Science layout, but hinges on Quarto Manuals’ /notebooks directory for its functionality.

/containers houses all container artifacts; .sif files are ignored;
/data uses 3 subfolders – inputs, interim, and outputs, where the first are staged using stagecoach, the interim is for ephemeral data that can be discarded, and outputs is used for data that ultimately gets versioned and shared;
/docs houses the docs for the project, generated by quarto render notebooks
/notebooks drives development of this manual
/scripts drives execution of this manual, including container runtime helpers


There aren’t any specific checks necessary before running this procedure.
You just need to ensure that the root directory for this repo is writable.


Run the following to materialize the necessary folder:
mkdir -p containers data/inputs data/intermediates data/outputs docs notebooks scripts

text:
This is a private health dataset. No data can be shared outside of authorized parties. This also means that any visualizations and tables must be strictly masked.
At present, this is enforced by project access on GitHub and by data access on FASRC. The project does originate from before TMT joined the team, so a lot of retroactive engineering is likely.

title: 6  Local Operator Environment
text:
6.1 What this does—and does not—provide
direnv is an optional command-line convenience for a Manual operator. It is not part of the scientific execution environment: the container runner starts with a clean environment, and Spack plus the container image define the R ABI, system libraries, and reproducible package installation.
The generated .envrc only helps an operator locate this checkout and invoke the isolated Manual render with a memorable command. It does not contain data locations, credentials, release parameters, library paths, or scientific dependencies.
This file deliberately does not set PATH, SPACK_VIEW, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, or PKG_CONFIG_PATH. Those variables cannot configure a clean container invocation and would blur the boundary between host-side engineering and scientific work. The runner and image establish the scientific environment inside Singularity. direnv adds only the existing generated scripts directory to PATH; it does not create a function, alias, shim, or additional implementation file.
Use the existing isolated-render command without its path for the normal Manual workflow:
For Slurm jobs, scripts, or systems without direnv, invoke scripts/render-isolated directly. That wrapper remains the one portable, auditable implementation; direnv only removes its path from an interactive shell.

title: 7  Bootstrap the Spack Builder
text:
The first container is a workshop, not the project runtime. It contains Rocky Linux 9 and a pinned Spack release, but no project packages. Quarto materializes this Manual; Singularity or Apptainer builds the small definition below into spack-builder.sif. The cluster’s Spack installation remains useful for inspection and troubleshooting, but is not allowed to resolve this project’s package graph.
This separates bootstrapping from project resolution. Later pages use this builder image to handle Spack work in Rocky 9; the final runtime image contains the resolved project view, not a mutable Spack installation.
The upstream Spack image supplies Spack under /opt/spack, but a Singularity image must declare its own runtime environment rather than relying on the Docker image entrypoint. The definition therefore adds /opt/spack/bin to PATH; spack --version is the first observable promise of this stage.

command -v quarto
command -v singularity


Bootstrap: docker
From: spack/rockylinux9:1.2.0

%environment
export SPACK_ROOT=/opt/spack
export PATH=/opt/spack/bin:${PATH}


mkdir -p artifacts/containers
singularity build --fakeroot artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif \
  containers/bootstrap/spack-builder.def


quarto render notebooks --profile emit --no-execute
singularity exec artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif spack --version
singularity exec artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif cat /etc/os-release
The successful image and the two commands above are the promised evidence for this stage: the workshop exists, runs Rocky 9, and has Spack available, but it does not yet claim to contain R or any project dependency.

title: 8  Declare the Native Runtime
text:
This page adds the project components to the empty workshop. spack.yaml is the reviewable declaration; it is deliberately not concretized or installed here. The next page turns this declaration into a Singularity recipe and builds the runtime inside the pinned Rocky 9 workshop.
The runtime uses the x86_64_v3 CPU baseline rather than the Sapphire Rapids build host. This preserves the broadly useful AVX2/FMA baseline while excluding AVX-512/VNNI, and applies the policy to every dependency rather than as a package-specific compiler-flag workaround.
targets loads igraph, whose artifact requires libglpk.so.40 and libflexiblas.so.3. glpk and flexiblas are therefore direct Spack specifications: OpenBLAS does not satisfy FlexiBLAS’s distinct SONAME. R packages remain project-local and are declared after the runtime exists with uvr.

spack:
  specs:
  - r@4.5.1
  - libxml2
  - icu4c
  - libx11
  - git
  - curl
  - openssl
  - libgit2
  - cmake
  - gmake
  - freetype
  - libjpeg-turbo
  - libpng
  - libtiff
  - libwebp
  - fontconfig
  - fribidi
  - harfbuzz
  - libuv
  - glpk
  - flexiblas
  view: true
  concretizer:
    unify: true
  packages:
    all:
      require:
      - target=x86_64_v3
  config:
    template_dirs:
    - $env/containers/templates
    - $spack/share/spack/templates
  container:
    format: singularity
    images:
      os: rockylinux:9
      spack: 1.2.0
    template: KiribatiBioMarkers.def.j2
    os_packages:
      final:
      - ca-certificates
      - findutils
      - gzip
      - tar
      - which
      - gcc
      - gcc-c++
      - make


quarto render notebooks --profile emit --no-execute
rg -n 'r@4.5.1|glpk|flexiblas|target=x86_64_v3|rockylinux:9' spack.yaml

title: 9  Customize and Build the Runtime
text:
This page has two explicit jobs. The Jinja template adds the small runtime contract that Spack’s standard Singularity recipe does not know about: the uvr executable and the environment variables that expose the Spack view. Then the commands below use the workshop from the Bootstrap page to render the final recipe and build the image.
This Manual uses singularity deliberately. Confirm that it is the container runtime available on the system before proceeding. If a site uses Apptainer, an operator should make that substitution consciously and use it consistently for recipe generation, image building, and later execution.

command -v singularity
test -r artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif


{% extends "container/singularity.def" %}

{% block build_stage %}
{{ super() }}
  set -euo pipefail
  UVR_VERSION=0.4.6
  QUARTO_VERSION=1.9.38
  curl --fail --location --show-error --output /tmp/uvr.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/nbafrank/uvr/releases/download/v${UVR_VERSION}/uvr-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz"
  mkdir -p /opt/uvr/bin
  tar -xzf /tmp/uvr.tar.gz -C /opt/uvr/bin
  rm -f /tmp/uvr.tar.gz
  /opt/uvr/bin/uvr --version | grep -Fx "uvr ${UVR_VERSION}"
  curl --fail --location --show-error --output /tmp/quarto.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-amd64.tar.gz"
  mkdir -p /opt/quarto
  tar -xzf /tmp/quarto.tar.gz -C /opt/quarto --strip-components=1
  rm -f /tmp/quarto.tar.gz
  /opt/quarto/bin/quarto --version | grep -Fx "${QUARTO_VERSION}"
{% endblock %}

{% block final_stage %}
{{ super() }}
%files from build
  /opt/uvr /opt/uvr
  /opt/quarto /opt/quarto
  /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock
%post
  set -eu
  ln -sf /opt/uvr/bin/uvr /usr/local/bin/uvr
  ln -sf /opt/quarto/bin/quarto /usr/local/bin/quarto
  cat >> "$SINGULARITY_ENVIRONMENT" <<'EOF'
unset R_HOME
export SPACK_VIEW=/opt/views/view
export PATH="/usr/local/bin:/opt/views/view/bin:${PATH}"
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="/opt/views/view/lib/pkgconfig:/opt/views/view/lib64/pkgconfig:/opt/views/view/share/pkgconfig:${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:-}"
export CPATH="/opt/views/view/include:${CPATH:-}"
export LIBRARY_PATH="/opt/views/view/lib:/opt/views/view/lib64:${LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="/opt/views/view/lib:/opt/views/view/lib64:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
export UVR_LIBRARY=/work/.uvr/library
export UVR_CACHE_DIR=/work/.uvr/cache
export R_LIBS_USER=/work/.uvr/library
export R_LIBS=/work/.uvr/library
EOF
%test
  set -eu
  command -v R
  command -v Rscript
  command -v uvr
  command -v quarto
  R --version
  uvr --version
  quarto --version | grep -Fx "1.9.38"
  test -r /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock
  test ! -e /opt/spack/bin/spack
{% endblock %}


Run this one command from the repository root inside your usual salloc work block; no sbatch file is required. It first asks the workshop to render the recipe, then builds that recipe; the second operation concretizes and installs the graph inside its pinned Rocky 9 build stage.
At the end of a work block, submit the same operation as a one-off, non-interactive job—without creating an sbatch file—by using sbatch --wrap. This does not replace the usual salloc workflow; it is only a way to leave this long-running build with Slurm.

mkdir -p containers/build artifacts/containers && singularity exec --cleanenv --bind "$PWD:/work" artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif /bin/bash -lc 'cd /work && spack -e . containerize > containers/build/kiribati-biomarkers.def' && singularity build --fakeroot artifacts/containers/kiribati-biomarkers.sif containers/build/kiribati-biomarkers.def


singularity exec artifacts/containers/kiribati-biomarkers.sif R --version
singularity exec artifacts/containers/kiribati-biomarkers.sif uvr --version
singularity exec artifacts/containers/kiribati-biomarkers.sif test -r /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock
singularity exec artifacts/containers/kiribati-biomarkers.sif test ! -e /opt/spack/bin/spack

title: 11  Run the Project Environment
text:
The runner is the only place that chooses a container implementation, selects the image, sets a clean host environment, and binds writable project state. The image’s %environment activates Spack R and the project-local uvr library. Slurm invokes this runner rather than reproducing mount decisions.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

project_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)
local_env="${project_dir}/containers/runtime/local.env"
if [[ -f "${local_env}" ]]; then
  set -a
  source "${local_env}"
  set +a
fi

runtime=${CONTAINER_RUNTIME:-apptainer}
if ! command -v "${runtime}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  runtime=singularity
fi
command -v "${runtime}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Neither apptainer nor singularity is available." >&2; exit 127; }

image=${KIRIBATI_BIOMARKERS_IMAGE:-"${project_dir}/artifacts/containers/kiribati-biomarkers.sif"}
test -r "${image}" || {
  echo "Container image not readable: ${image}" >&2
  echo "Build it with the Customize and Build the Runtime procedure or set KIRIBATI_BIOMARKERS_IMAGE." >&2
  exit 1
}

mkdir -p "${project_dir}/.container-home" "${project_dir}/.container-tmp" "${project_dir}/.uvr/library" "${project_dir}/.uvr/cache"
if (( $# == 0 )); then
  set -- /bin/bash -i
fi

exec "${runtime}" exec --cleanenv \
  --bind "${project_dir}:/work" \
  --bind "${project_dir}/.container-tmp:/tmp" \
  --home "${project_dir}/.container-home:/home/rse" \
  "${image}" \
  /bin/bash -lc 'set -e; cd /work; exec "$@"' \
  kiribati-biomarkers "$@"

title: 12  Stage Inputs
text:
12.1 Targets declared in this stage
Before running the input-provenance pipeline, stage the source materials at the repository input boundary. The pipeline has exactly two prerequisites:
The manifest records the staging context, while data/inputs/ contains the files that are actually available to this project.
The project-root _targets.R tangles this notebook together with the curation and release-packaging notebooks. Each assignment in the disabled R chunks below becomes one target; the chunks are disabled so that reading or rendering the Manual never inspects protected inputs. This stage declares the two file targets that form the input boundary.
For this project, out input data is part of the Google Drive Rclone tree.

title: 12  Stage Inputs

#| format: file
pipeline_stagecoach_manifest_path <- here::here("stagecoach_manifest.yml")

pipeline_raw_input_files_paths <- {

  input_dir <- here::here("data", "inputs")
  if (!dir.exists(input_dir)) {
    stop("Staged input directory is missing: ", input_dir)
  }

  inputs <- list.files(
    input_dir,

text:
In this stage of the pipeline, we need to identify and fix NAs eminating from the source data that was merged with HIES and Dharma data upstream. From JZM email:

Presumably something with nas due to village or gender?
Dharma had nas in several of these and, where possible, I think we populated with hies data (I think village and community may be the same thing) However, there may still be nas if the original dharma didn’t have them! To check if the underlying issue was already in the data you probably have to go to the level 0 and level 1 excel spreadsheets you shared with me originally

The following is what I believe to be the corresponding code of those changes. What I think would be a good next strategy is to identify each of the CSVs/XLSX files and ensure they’re available.

kiri_data<-read.csv(file="kiribati_cleandata_mergedHIES.csv",header=T): ✅

book <- read_excel("/Users/heatherkelahan/Desktop/Kiribati/Book1.xlsx") ❌

The available files are in the existing Goldenetal repo; I haven’t found any of the others in our available Google Drive. If this code is indeed the correct one to repair the NAs, I’ll need the 4 missing files to run it from top to tail.
I also asked myself if I won’t need the full set of files, and maybe the merge gets written out before needing island_samples etc.; what I found is that this script actually has no record of write.csv or related writers.
So, I also looked into the folder Health data cleaning, exploration and merging to HIES and found similar mentions of HIES in a notebook, but this folder notably has no input files, but a folder labelled cleaned data, which seems counterfactual to our investigation. That being said, it does have the following files:

kiribati_data_final_level0.csv ✅ (available but not clear where they came from)
kiribati_data_final_level1.csv ✅

The fact that they’re in cleaned but used as input to a cleaning script elsewhere makes me suspicious that this is a circular dataset (it overwrites itself). This is particularly important as they are used as inputs to the file Kiribati_merging_HEIS_Dharma.Rmd. The question, then is, how did level0 and level1 materialize without a write.csv anywhere?
I believe those files are the ones JZM is referring to in her correspondance.

text:
14.2 Curation rules migrated from the legacy vignette
The release derives age in months from interview date and date of birth, drops nonpositive derived ages, and replaces the source identifier with its MD5 digest. The small release retains only approved village_id and rururb; it does not contain literal community or island names. Thus the approved metadata, rather than this pipeline, supplies the non-reversible location key (i.e., the data remains non-identifiable outside of the pipeline operator).

14.3 Simple Pipeline
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(lubridate)
Our simple pipeline takes the raw data and modifies required column names for release. No other major curation happens here.
Notably, this is separate from Manual operation — it doesn’t require a procedure block because it is a targets managed stage.
First, list the biomarker columns we got from CG:
biomarker_output_columns_vec <- c(
  "DOB_HIES", "date_of_interview", "hhld_id_hm_basic__id", "L1_q61_hdl",

  "triglycerides_corrected", "systolic_corrected", "diastolic_corrected",

We create a small function here to convert an identifier to a hash, preserving PHI.
hash_identifier <- function(identifier) {
  vapply(as.character(identifier), digest::digest, character(1))
}

14.5 Derive age and record source-quality evidence

    mutate(

title: 14  Curate Release
text:
14.6 Construct the two de-identified releases
The slimmed release contains clinical measures and status fields. The small release joins approved non-identifying location metadata and omits literal community and island names.
biomarker_clean_df <- biomarker_ptx_age_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(age_in_months), age_in_months > 0) %>%
  transmute(
    uid = hash_identifier(hhld_id_hm_basic__id),
    hdl = L1_q61_hdl, ldl = ldl_corrected,
    tc = tc_corrected, pulse = pulse_corrected,
    glucose = glucose_corrected,
    triglycerides = triglycerides_corrected,
    systolic = systolic_corrected, diastolic = diastolic_corrected,
    temperature = temperature_correctedF,
    hemoglobin = hemoglobin_corrected, hematocrit = hematocrit_corrected,
    diabetes = diabetes_corrected, age_group = age_group,
    fever = fever, BloodPressure_status = BloodPressure_status,
    Glucose_status = Glucose_status, anemia_status = anemia_status,
    cholesterol_status = cholesterol_status,
    triglycerides_status = triglycerides_status,
    diabetes_status = diabetes_status, gender = gender_HIES,
    age_in_months
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor), uid = as.character(uid))
demog_clean_df <- biomarker_ptx_age_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(age_in_months), age_in_months > 0) %>%
  transmute(
    uid = hash_identifier(hhld_id_hm_basic__id), age_in_months,
    gender = L1_q3_gender,
    community = L1_q125_which_community_are_you_in,
    island = L1_q124_which_island_are_we_on
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    select(demog_ptx_village_raw_df, village, island, village_id, rururb),
    by = c("community" = "village", "island" = "island")
  ) %>%
  select(uid, age_in_months, gender, village_id, rururb) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor), uid = as.character(uid))

title: 15  Package Release
text:
15.1 Describe the biomarker resource
This page is the source of truth for release serialization. It turns the two curated participant-grain targets into a single Frictionless Data Package. The package descriptor carries the data dictionaries as field descriptions, so the release does not require separately maintained dictionary CSV files.
create_schema() infers field types and factor enumerations. This target adds the release-specific descriptions and fails if the description set and curated columns diverge.

title: 15  Package Release
text:
biomarker_ptx_dictionary_field_described_list <- {
  biomarker_description_chr <- c(
    uid = "De-identified record identifier",
    hdl = "HDL cholesterol",
    ldl = "LDL cholesterol",
    tc = "Total cholesterol",
    pulse = "Pulse",
    glucose = "Glucose",
    triglycerides = "Triglycerides",
    systolic = "Systolic blood pressure",
    diastolic = "Diastolic blood pressure",
    temperature = "Temperature in Fahrenheit",
    hemoglobin = "Hemoglobin level",
    hematocrit = "Percentage of red blood cells",
    diabetes = "HbA1c level",
    age_group = "Age group",
    fever = "Fever recorded",
    BloodPressure_status = "Blood pressure status",
    Glucose_status = "Glucose status",
    anemia_status = "Anemia status",
    cholesterol_status = "Cholesterol status",
    triglycerides_status = "Triglycerides status",
    diabetes_status = "Diabetes status",
    gender = "Gender",
    age_in_months = "Age in months at interview"
  )
  biomarker_schema_list <- frictionless::create_schema(
    biomarker_clean_df
  )
  biomarker_field_name_chr <- vapply(
    biomarker_schema_list$fields,
    `[[`,
    character(1),
    "name"
  )
  if (!setequal(names(biomarker_description_chr), biomarker_field_name_chr)) {
    stop("Biomarker field descriptions do not match the curated columns.")
  }
  biomarker_schema_list$fields <- lapply(
    biomarker_schema_list$fields,
    function(field_list) {
      field_list$description <- unname(
        biomarker_description_chr[[field_list$name]]
      )
      field_list
    }
  )

  biomarker_schema_list
}

16.1 Register the notebook graph
This page shows how to register the input-provenance, curation, and packaging notebooks in the project-root target script. The graph itself is declared, with its explanatory narrative, in those notebooks. Scientific execution is a separate, explicit container-runtime operation.
In the repository-root _targets.R created by targets::use_targets(), replace its example targets with the following pipeline list. Only notebooks containing target declarations are registered.
_targets.R is deliberately maintained at the project root, alongside the other project-level configuration. It is the single entry point that targets::tar_make() reads; the pipeline/ directory holds notebooks, not a second targets project.
The command is intentionally not a Quarto render hook. It fails if the scientific pipeline fails, and it runs with the container’s Spack R runtime and project-local package library rather than the host environment.

)

schema_description_complete <- function(package_list, resource_name_chr) {
  resource_schema_list <- frictionless::schema(
    package_list,
    resource_name_chr
  )
  all(vapply(
    resource_schema_list$fields,
    function(field_list) {
      !is.null(field_list$description) && nzchar(field_list$description)
    },
    logical(1)
  ))
}

  schema_description_complete(release_package_list, "demog_ptx")
